fetched_contents.text: Accounting disclosures and stock price efficiency: Evidence from mandatory IFRS adoption 1. Introduction Stock price efficiency is crucial for capital markets, as it influences the real economy (Morck et al., 1990), provides signals for economic resource allocation (Wurgler, 2000), and supports firm investments - particularly when relying on equity financing (Baker et al., 2003).1 Financial markets worldwide have grown increasingly integrated due to the removal of capital controls and policy initiatives promoting market integration, such as opening domestic markets to foreign investors, lifting foreign exchange restrictions, and fostering international trade through free trade agreements. These actions should, in theory, enhance stock price efficiency. Indeed, financial integration has been shown to lower firms' cost of capital (Henry, 2000a), increase corporate investment (Henry, 2000b), and stimulate economic growth (Guiso et al., 2004). These outcomes are consistent with improved stock price efficiency. A key driver of this market integration is the global harmonization of accounting standards (Dhaliwal et al., 2019), suggesting that the adoption of International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) should also promote stock price efficiency. This study provides a fundamental and direct test of IFRS efficacy by examining whether its adoption enhances market efficiency – a core component of the IFRS mission. Our research makes two important contributions. First, we introduce a novel efficiency test that evaluates IFRS effectiveness at the highest level of its stated goals. Prior studies have primarily examined theoretical constructs and empirical measures of reporting quality tied to IFRS' qualitative characteristics (e.g., Barth, Landsman and Lang, 2008, Barth, Landsman, Lang and Williams, 2012; Daske et al., 2008; Neel, 2017), generally supporting the hypothesis that IFRS improves financial reporting quality. However, our study addresses two critical gaps in this literature. The first gap arises from mixed prior findings (e.g., Daske et al., 2008; De George et al., 2016; Leuz & Wysocki, 2016). Our results shift the balance of evidence in favor of IFRS adoption, over pre-existing GAAPs, constituting a net improvement in financial reporting. The second gap stems from prior research's focus on accounting quality linked to IFRS' qualitative characteristics. While improved financial reporting quality likely enhances stock price efficiency, this is not guaranteed, as information may still reach prices through alternative channels. Our study provides a direct test of whether the adoption of IFRS improves financial reporting in a way that improves stock price efficiency, thereby providing unambiguous evidence of its benefits. The second contribution lies in the efficiency test itself, which captures the full scope of the information system shift from domestic GAAP to IFRS. Unlike prior work, which often examines specific signals tied to summary financial statement measures (typically earnings), our approach is agnostic to the information source (whether financial statements, footnotes, or other disclosures), as long as it potentially enhances stock price efficiency. This method allows us to assess the aggregate informational impact of IFRS as a complete system, even when changes are too broad for any single metric (i.e., earnings) to serve as a definitive signal. This efficiency-based approach also represents a methodological innovation, enabling researchers to evaluate the collective impact of a major regulatory change—such as the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB) standards or the new IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements. Furthermore, our approach tests at a level corresponding to the highest level of the International Accounting Standards Board's (IASB) goals and objectives. The IASB defines its mission as to develop high-quality IFRS “standards that bring transparency, accountability and efficiency to financial markets around the world” (IASB, 2018, SP1.5). In its Conceptual Framework, the IASB then describes the objective of general-purpose financial reporting as “to provide financial information about the reporting entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders, and other creditors in making decisions relating to providing resources to the entity” (IASB, 2018, 1.2). The Conceptual framework subsequently develops characteristics of financial information that fulfill the objective as “(t)he qualitative characteristics of useful financial information … that are likely to be most useful to the existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors for making decisions about the reporting entity on the basis of information in its financial report (financial information)” (2.1). There are two primary characteristics, relevance and faithful representation and four enhancing characteristics: comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability (2.4–2.36). Collectively, these elements form an implicit informational hierarchy within IFRS. Measurement approaches for information asymmetry

Researchers commonly operationalize information asymmetry in IFRS adoption studies using market microstructure proxies rather than direct reporting-quality measures. One primary study explicitly uses “market microstructure proxies for information asymmetry” to examine the effects of IFRS adoption on information levels in the Spanish stock market [N1-F1]. Another source notes that empirical studies associate high trading volume with lower levels of information asymmetry and increased stock liquidity, suggesting that liquidity-related variables are often used as proxies for information asymmetry [N1-R2]. In addition, the literature on accounting disclosures and stock price efficiency indicates that information asymmetry is linked to analyst forecast accuracy and disclosure quality more generally [N3-F3].

The most direct accounting link is that IFRS adoption is expected to improve transparency and comparability, which should reduce information asymmetry and thus improve the information environment for market participants [N1-F1]. The same source emphasizes that researchers control for conventional determinants of information asymmetry and firms’ characteristics influencing their information environments [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that information-asymmetry proxies are not treated as standalone measures of accounting quality; instead, they are interpreted as signals that reflect the broader information environment shaped by accounting standards [N1-F1].

Studies in the provided evidence distinguish between pre-adoption and post-adoption changes, especially when examining a mandatory switch from local standards to IFRS. The Spanish study is explicitly a pre- and post-adoption analysis of IFRS adoption [N1-F1], and the literature review notes that early IFRS studies often examined changes around the adoption date [N5-F4]. This makes the measure sensitive to adoption timing, but also means that the effect is usually compared against a baseline period before the standard change [N1-F1][N5-F4].

Cross-sectional and firm-level heterogeneity matter because the evidence shows that researchers examine the effects of IFRS adoption across firms and across countries, and they often highlight cross-sectional differences in adoption quality and economic consequences [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The literature review also notes that many studies focus on average effects rather than cross-sectional differences, but recent work increasingly examines firm-level heterogeneity [N6-R2]. In particular, the liquidity study finds that liquidity benefits are more pronounced for firms with lower liquidity, implying that heterogeneity across firms can amplify or modify the observed effect [N2-F2]. For information asymmetry, the evidence suggests that heterogeneity across firms matters because different firms face different enforcement environments and information environments [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The broader point is that effect magnitudes are not uniform across firms or countries, and heterogeneity can strengthen or bias inferences if not properly controlled [N6-R2][N6-R5].

Overall, common proxies for information asymmetry include market microstructure measures, trading volume, and related liquidity indicators, while the link to accounting disclosure or analyst forecast accuracy is indirect but well established in the literature [N1-F1][N1-R2][N3-F3]. Most studies use pre-post or adoption-event designs, and they are increasingly attentive to firm-level and cross-sectional heterogeneity [N1-F1][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R5].

Measurement approaches for liquidity

Researchers measure liquidity effects of IFRS adoption using a range of market liquidity indicators, with bid-ask spreads and turnover being especially prominent. The liquidity study explicitly uses factor analysis and four liquidity proxies: the modified LOT measure, quoted bid-ask spreads, proportion of zero return days, and another spread-related measure [N2-F2]. It also notes that earlier research finds liquidity increases of between three and six percent in the year of IFRS adoption, indicating that liquidity is often measured as a continuous variable rather than as a binary or qualitative signal [N2-F2]. This makes liquidity measurement in IFRS adoption studies typically time-series in nature, with liquidity indicators tracked across periods before and after adoption [N2-F2].

Liquidity is linked to accounting transparency and information quality through the expectation that more transparent reporting reduces information asymmetry and, therefore, transaction costs and the cost of capital [N2-F2]. The study explains that increased comparability, consistency, and transparency in accounting practices were expected to better facilitate decision making by market participants and reduce opportunities for firms to exploit favorable accounting practices [N2-F2]. In effect, liquidity is treated as a downstream effect of information quality: improved information should make trading easier, reduce search frictions, and lower the cost of capital [N2-F2]. The study also finds evidence consistent with liquidity benefits being attributable to IFRS adoption, especially for the lowest liquidity firms [N2-F2].

Studies in the evidence use both cross-sectional and time-series liquidity indicators. The liquidity study explicitly compares cross-sectional differences in changes in liquidity for Canadian firms before and after IFRS adoption [N2-R3]. It also uses firm-level pre-post data and quantile regression to examine how liquidity benefits vary across liquidity deciles [N2-F2]. This combination of cross-sectional and time-series approaches allows researchers to assess both the average liquidity effect and the heterogeneity of that effect [N2-R3][N2-F2]. In addition, the literature review notes that IFRS adoption studies often examine average effects, but recent work increasingly explores firm-level differences [N6-R2], reinforcing the importance of cross-sectional heterogeneity.

Heterogeneity across firms and countries changes liquidity responses. The evidence shows that liquidity benefits are greater for less liquid firms [N2-F2], and the study also finds some evidence of liquidity benefits for non-EU firms from low regulatory quality countries [N2-F2]. This implies that the magnitude of the liquidity effect is not uniform and depends on the pre-adoption liquidity position and the institutional environment. The literature review further notes that many IFRS adoption studies examine average effects rather than cross-sectional differences, but recent work increasingly does so [N6-R2]. In other words, heterogeneity can strengthen the observed effect when the treatment is more beneficial for firms with higher information frictions or weaker enforcement [N2-F2][N6-R2].

Overall, liquidity is measured using bid-ask spreads, turnover, and related microstructure proxies, with studies often combining cross-sectional and time-series indicators [N2-F2][N2-R3]. Liquidity is interpreted as a signal of accounting transparency and information quality, and heterogeneity across firms and countries can change the effect magnitude [N2-F2][N6-R2].

Measurement approaches for valuation

Valuation effects of IFRS adoption are measured using stock returns, price-to-book ratios, and price-to-earnings ratios, with the evidence emphasizing stock price efficiency as a central valuation proxy. The valuation study on accounting disclosures and stock price efficiency reports that mandatory adoption of IFRS enhances stock price efficiency, and that results remain robust after controlling for various factors [N3-F3]. It also notes that prior studies have examined theoretical constructs and empirical measures of reporting quality tied to IFRS’ qualitative characteristics, but this study provides a direct test of IFRS efficacy by examining whether adoption improves market efficiency [N3-F3]. A related study on Indonesia finds evidence that IFRS adoption reduces stock price synchronicity, which is consistent with improved information efficiency [N3-R2]. Another study on the impact of IFRS adoption on stock price informativeness supports the view that IFRS adoption affects stock price informativeness [N3-R4]. Together, these sources suggest that valuation is measured not only by raw stock price changes but also by broader informational properties of prices.

Valuation responses are interpreted as information efficiency signals. The valuation study argues that stock price efficiency is crucial for capital markets and reflects whether financial information is incorporated into prices quickly and accurately [N3-F3]. It further notes that improved financial reporting quality likely enhances stock price efficiency, but this is not guaranteed because information may still reach prices through alternative channels [N3-F3]. The study treats IFRS adoption as a test of whether the information system shift from domestic GAAP to IFRS improves the informational environment and therefore improves stock price efficiency [N3-F3]. This framing means that valuation responses are read as signals of whether the market is better able to process and value firm information after IFRS adoption [N3-F3].

Methodological differences across event studies and fixed-effects designs are evident in the evidence. The valuation study introduces a novel efficiency test and is described as a direct test of IFRS efficacy rather than relying on a single earnings-based signal [N3-F3]. It also notes that prior work often examines specific signals tied to summary financial statement measures, typically earnings, whereas this approach is more general and agnostic to the information source [N3-F3]. In contrast, the literature review notes that early IFRS studies often examined effects around the adoption date, but later work increasingly uses more refined identification strategies [N5-F4]. This suggests that valuation studies may use event-study designs when the adoption date is clear, while fixed-effects or panel designs may be used when researchers want to control for firm-specific or country-specific factors [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Heterogeneity across firms or countries affects valuation responses. The literature review notes that many IFRS adoption studies examine average effects, but recent work increasingly examines firm-level differences [N6-R2]. The valuation study itself provides evidence on whether IFRS adoption enhances market efficiency, implying that the effect may vary across countries and firms [N3-F3]. The evidence also suggests that cross-sectional differences in adoption quality and economic consequences matter, and that heterogeneity can change the interpretation of effects [N6-R2][N6-R5]. In particular, because IFRS adoption is often studied in countries with different legal and institutional regimes, valuation responses are likely to differ across jurisdictions [N5-F4][N6-R2].

Overall, valuation is measured using stock returns, price-to-book, and price-to-earnings ratios, with stock price efficiency as a central valuation proxy [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4]. Valuation responses are interpreted as information efficiency signals, and methodological differences exist between event-study and fixed-effects designs [N3-F3][N5-F4]. Heterogeneity across firms and countries can change valuation responses, and the literature increasingly recognizes that effects are not uniform [N6-R2][N6-R5].

Broader empirical design and validity issues

Identification strategies and causal inference problems are central to IFRS adoption research. The evidence shows that researchers frequently use staggered treatment timing and event-study approaches to assess the impact of policy changes on corporate outcomes [N4-R2][N4-R4]. The literature review also notes that IFRS adoption has provided an unprecedented experiment for studying accounting standard setting, but the effect on academic research has gone beyond simply providing a useful context [N5-F4]. This implies that the standard identification problem is not only whether IFRS adoption caused the outcome, but also whether the observed effect can be separated from other concurrent changes, such as regulatory enforcement changes or other policy reforms [N5-F4].

Limitations such as endogeneity, omitted variables, and reverse causation are well documented. The literature review explicitly discusses empirical challenges faced by researchers in the IFRS setting and highlights the limitations of drawing causal conclusions [N5-F4]. It also notes that many early studies tend to ignore caveats about the role of IFRS in causing observed outcomes [N5-F4]. The endogeneity problem is especially important because the review states that IFRS adoption may be correlated with other concurrent changes, including enforcement improvements and other factors [N5-F4]. This makes it difficult to isolate the true causal effect of IFRS adoption alone. The endogeneity discussion in the literature review also stresses that the initial evidence could be affected by publication bias, as significant results are more likely to be published than studies that fail to reject the null [N5-F4]. This raises a methodological limitation: the literature may overstate positive effects because only significant results are visible.

Researchers address sample selection and timing issues through identification strategies and careful specification. The event-study literature provides a straightforward approach to time-varying treatment effects and can be adapted to staggered treatment designs [N4-R4]. The literature review also notes that IFRS adoption studies often examine effects around the adoption date, which helps address timing issues [N5-F4]. However, the same review emphasizes that many studies do not clarify whether “IFRS mandate” or “IFRS adoption” refers simply to the adoption of new standards or includes concurrent improvements in enforcement [N5-F4]. This ambiguity can lead to sample-selection problems if researchers do not properly separate the treatment from other concurrent changes. The literature review also notes that some recent studies attempt to narrow down the sources of observed benefits and conclude that at least some earlier documented benefits are not driven by the adoption of new accounting standards per se [N5-F4].

Cross-sectional and firm-level heterogeneity can bias or strengthen inferences. The literature review states that many studies examine average effects, but recent work increasingly examines firm-level differences [N6-R2]. The evidence also shows that heterogeneity matters because liquidity benefits are greater for less liquid firms [N2-F2], and that cross-sectional differences in adoption quality and economic consequences are important [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The same review notes that the simultaneous mandatory adoption of IFRS by a large number of countries has created an opportunity for cross-country comparative studies, but that effects can vary across institutional and legal regimes [N5-F4]. This means that heterogeneity can both strengthen inference when the treatment is more effective in certain subgroups and bias inference if researchers do not properly account for it.

Overall, IFRS adoption studies rely on event-study and staggered-difference-in-differences designs to estimate causal effects, but they face serious endogeneity, omitted-variables, and reverse-causation problems [N4-R2][N4-R4][N5-F4]. Researchers address sample selection and timing by using adoption-event designs and careful specification, but the literature often underestimates the role of concurrent changes and publication bias [N5-F4]. Cross-sectional and firm-level heterogeneity can both strengthen and bias inferences, depending on how the effect varies across firms and countries [N6-R2][N2-F2][N5-F4].

## How researchers measure the effects of IFRS adoption on stock market variables

Researchers measure the effects of IFRS adoption on stock market variables such as information asymmetry, liquidity, and valuation by combining **microstructure proxies, accounting quality signals, and valuation efficiency indicators**, while also relying on **identification strategies** to infer causality. The evidence across the branch reports shows that these measures are not isolated; they are deeply tied to the information environment created by IFRS, and researchers increasingly recognize that effects vary across firms and countries.

### 1) Information asymmetry: market microstructure proxies and disclosure-related signals

The most common way researchers operationalize information asymmetry is through **market microstructure proxies** rather than direct accounting-quality measures. One study explicitly uses “market microstructure proxies for information asymmetry” to examine the effects of IFRS adoption on information levels in the Spanish stock market [N1-F1]. Another source notes that empirical studies associate **high trading volume** with **lower levels of information asymmetry** and **increased stock liquidity**, indicating that liquidity-related variables are often used as proxies for information asymmetry [N1-R2]. A broader valuation study also links information asymmetry to **analyst forecast accuracy** and **disclosure quality** more generally, reinforcing the idea that information asymmetry is not measured directly from accounting statements alone, but through how markets interpret them [N3-F3].

Researchers interpret these proxies as signals of the broader information environment. IFRS adoption is expected to improve **transparency** and **comparability**, which should reduce information asymmetry and improve the information environment for market participants [N1-F1]. In practice, this means that studies often control for conventional determinants of information asymmetry and firms’ characteristics that influence their information environments [N1-F1]. In other words, information-asymmetry proxies are treated as downstream indicators of the accounting disclosure environment, not as direct measures of reporting quality [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Studies usually distinguish between **pre-adoption and post-adoption changes**. The Spanish study is an explicit pre- and post-adoption analysis of IFRS adoption [N1-F1], and the literature review notes that early IFRS studies often examined changes around the adoption date [N5-F4]. The literature review notes that many IFRS adoption studies examine average effects, but recent work increasingly examines **firm-level differences** [N6-R2]. The evidence also shows that liquidity benefits are more pronounced for firms with lower liquidity, implying that heterogeneity across firms can amplify or modify the observed effect [N2-F2]. For information asymmetry, the evidence suggests that heterogeneity across firms matters because different firms face different enforcement environments and information environments [N1-F1][N6-R5]. In short, the effect is not uniform across firms or countries, and heterogeneity can strengthen or bias inferences if not properly controlled [N6-R2][N6-R5].

The study also finds evidence consistent with liquidity benefits being attributable to IFRS adoption, especially for the lowest liquidity firms [N2-F2].

Studies use both **cross-sectional and time-series liquidity indicators**. The liquidity study explicitly compares **cross-sectional differences in changes in liquidity** for Canadian firms before and after IFRS adoption [N2-R3]. It also uses firm-level pre-post data and quantile regression to examine how liquidity benefits vary across liquidity deciles [N2-F2]. Taken together, researchers measure the effects of IFRS adoption on stock market variables using a layered approach:

- **Valuation** is measured using **stock returns, price-to-book, price-to-earnings ratios, and stock price efficiency indicators**, interpreted as signals of **information efficiency** [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R4].
